label: Acapulco to Manila
source: Schurz, The Manila Galleon (1939); Flynn and Giráldez, "Born with a 'Silver Spoon': The Origin of World Trade in 1571," Journal of World History 6:2 (1995). Silver west. The lane ran near 13°N by the Marianas (Guam a regular stop from the 1660s), in by the San Bernardino Strait.
qc_note: DRAFT, not reviewed. The galleons went out and came back on different lanes. Drafted as two lines with no heads (a path: trade), direction in the name. The alternative is one line with heads at both ends. Owner to choose.

label: Manila to Acapulco
source: Schurz, The Manila Galleon (1939); Flynn and Giráldez, "Born with a 'Silver Spoon': The Origin of World Trade in 1571," Journal of World History 6:2 (1995). Silks and porcelain east. Urdaneta's return route (1565): north-east with the westerlies to the latitudes of Japan, landfall near Cape Mendocino, then down the coast. The open-ocean lane far north of the line drawn here has no gazetteer waypoint; Point Reyes, Point Conception, Cabo San Lucas and Cabo Corrientes are capes that keep the coastal run at sea, not recorded stops.

label: Fujian junks
source: Schurz, The Manila Galleon (1939); Flynn and Giráldez, "Born with a 'Silver Spoon': The Origin of World Trade in 1571," Journal of World History 6:2 (1995); Flynn and Giráldez (1995). Chinese junks brought silk and porcelain from Yuegang (Moon Harbor, opened to private trade 1567) to Spanish Manila (from 1571) for American silver.
qc_note: DRAFT, not reviewed. Yuegang has no coordinate on Wikidata, so the line starts at Zhangzhou, the prefecture it belonged to. The end year is a placeholder (the galleons' end); the junk trade outlived them. Owner to set.

label: Potosí silver
source: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Flynn and Giráldez (1995); Haring, Trade and Navigation between Spain and the Indies (1918). Potosí's silver found 1545; carried by llama and mule to Arica for the sea to Callao.
qc_note: DRAFT, not reviewed. Dates: 1545 is the find, not this road's first use; 1739 is the last of the galleons this leg fed. Owner to set.

label: to Panama
source: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Flynn and Giráldez (1995); Haring, Trade and Navigation between Spain and the Indies (1918). The South Sea fleet carried Peru's silver from Callao to Panama for the isthmus crossing. Paracas, Punta Pariñas and Cabo San Lorenzo are capes keeping the line off the coast, not recorded stops.

label: across the isthmus
source: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Flynn and Giráldez (1995); Haring, Trade and Navigation between Spain and the Indies (1918). Mule trains across the isthmus to the Caribbean fair, at Portobelo from 1597 (Nombre de Dios before).

label: the galleons to Seville
source: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Flynn and Giráldez (1995); Haring, Trade and Navigation between Spain and the Indies (1918). The Tierra Firme galleons by Cartagena and Havana to Seville; the Indies trade moved to Cádiz in 1717, and the last galleons sailed c. 1739.
qc_note: DRAFT, not reviewed. After 1717 the end of the line is Cádiz, not Seville: a second row if the 1750 map needs it.

label: Mexican silver
source: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Flynn and Giráldez (1995); Haring, Trade and Navigation between Spain and the Indies (1918). Zacatecas silver (found 1546) by road to Mexico City and down to Veracruz for the New Spain fleet.
qc_note: DRAFT, not reviewed. Dates: 1546 is the find; 1778 the end of the fleet system, not of the road. Owner to set.

label: the New Spain fleet
source: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Flynn and Giráldez (1995); Haring, Trade and Navigation between Spain and the Indies (1918). The annual fleet (flota) from Veracruz by Havana to Seville under the convoy system of the 1560s.

label: road to Acapulco
source: Schurz, The Manila Galleon (1939); Flynn and Giráldez, "Born with a 'Silver Spoon': The Origin of World Trade in 1571," Journal of World History 6:2 (1995). The road from Mexico City to Acapulco carried silver to the galleon and Asian goods inland.

label: Enslaved Africans to Brazil
source: Eltis and Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010); Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (slavevoyages.org); Alencastro, The Trade in the Living (2018). West Central Africa to Brazil, the largest single flow of the trade: from Luanda (founded 1576) until Brazil's ban of 1850. Ports joined, not a track; width does not show numbers.
qc_note: DRAFT, not reviewed. Forced migration: rust with an open head (grammar). Which flows a lesson shows, and their names, are the owner's.

label: Enslaved Africans to Jamaica
source: Eltis and Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010); Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (slavevoyages.org). The Gold Coast and the British Caribbean: Cape Coast Castle English from 1664, Jamaica from 1655; Britain abolished its trade in 1807. Cape Palmas is a waypoint keeping the line off the coast.

label: goods to West Africa
source: Eltis and Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010); Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (slavevoyages.org); Morgan, Slavery, Atlantic Trade and the British Economy, 1660–1800 (2000). Liverpool's first recorded slaving voyage 1699. St George's Channel, Cape Finisterre, the Cape Verde islands and Cape Palmas are waypoints keeping the line at sea.
qc_note: DRAFT, not reviewed. The "triangular trade" as three legs: this line, the forced migration to Jamaica, and the return. Owner to say whether a lesson needs it, and which home port (Bristol and London led before Liverpool).

label: sugar to Britain
source: Eltis and Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010); Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (slavevoyages.org); Morgan (2000).
